messages.content: My doctor says the screening test she ordered is 99% sensitive and 95% specific, and I just tested positive. The condition affects about 1 in 100 people like me. I assumed a positive means roughly a 99% chance I have it. Is that right?

Almost everyone makes that assumption, and it is wrong in an instructive way. Sensitivity is the probability of a positive given you have the condition. What you want is the reverse: the probability you have it given a positive. Let me build the picture with 10,000 people like you.
About 100 of the 10,000 actually have the condition. Of those, the test catches 99%:
Now the part everyone forgets: the 9,900 healthy people. A 95% specific test still flags 5% of them:

So out of 10,000 people, 594 test positive — but only 99 of them actually have the condition. A positive result means roughly a 16.7% chance, not 99%.

The test did not lie to you. The 99% sensitivity describes how the test behaves on people who are sick; your question is about people who test positive, and that group is dominated by false alarms from the huge healthy majority, because the condition is rare. This is exactly why a positive screening result is normally followed by a different, confirmatory test before anyone talks about treatment. Bring these numbers to your doctor — a positive here is a reason to test further, not a diagnosis.

Follow-up to the screening question: same test (99% sensitive, 95% specific), but now it is used in a specialist clinic where about 20% of the referred patients actually turn out to have the condition. A patient there tests positive. What is the chance now?
Same test, same positive result — but a very different starting population. Per 10,000 clinic patients:
And the healthy 8,000 still produce false positives at 5%:

Now a positive means about an 83% chance — up from 16.7% in general screening, with the identical test and the identical result.

Nothing about the test changed. What changed is the base rate: the clinic's referral process (symptoms, history, a GP's suspicion) already filtered the population before the test was run, so the positives are drawn from a pool where the condition is common. A test result is never a property of the test alone; it is the test acting on a prior probability. When someone quotes you a test's accuracy, the first question is always: accurate in which population?

Our mail provider says 40% of incoming mail is spam. Their filter catches 98% of spam, but it also flags 2% of legitimate mail as spam. For every 1,000 messages, what actually lands in the junk folder, and how much of the junk folder is really spam?
Let me run the 1,000 messages through the filter's two error rates.
That is the spam caught. The legitimate 600 messages contribute their own mistakes:

The junk folder holds 404 messages: 392 real spam and 12 legitimate ones — so the folder is about 97% pure, which sounds excellent. But read the numbers in the other direction too, because each direction is a different person's problem. For a legitimate sender, the filter means a 2% chance of being junked — that is the invoice or job offer that never gets seen. And 8 spam messages per 1,000 slip through to the inbox. A single '98% accurate' figure hides all three facts; the counts per 1,000 make the trade-offs visible enough to argue about sensibly.

A headline says a new blood test for a serious disease is '99% accurate'. My grandfather was screened at a community health fair and tested positive. The whole family is panicking. What should we actually make of it?

Please take a breath: at a general screening, a positive on even an excellent test is usually a false alarm, and the headline number is the reason people misjudge it.

'99% accurate' collapses two different rates into one slogan and ignores how rare the disease is in a walk-in population. Work it through with plausible figures — say the disease affects 1 in 1,000 screened people, the test catches essentially every case, and it falsely flags 5% of healthy people. In 100,000 screenings: 100 people have the disease and (nearly) all test positive. The other 99,900 are healthy, and 5% of them is 4,995 false positives. So the positive pool is about 100 real cases against 4,995 false alarms — a positive means roughly a 2% chance, not 99%.

That is not a defect in the test; it is arithmetic. Rare condition plus huge healthy majority means false positives outnumber true ones. The correct response to your grandfather's result is exactly what screening programs are designed for: a prompt follow-up with a different, more specific confirmatory test, which operates on a much higher base rate because the first positive already filtered the pool. Worry is understandable — but the number to carry into that appointment is 'about 1 in 50', not '99% certain'.

Our company does workplace drug testing. Roughly 0.5% of employees use the substance. The test is 99% sensitive and 98% specific. An employee just tested positive and HR wants to fire him on the spot. What is the probability he actually used?
Before anyone is fired, run the counts. Take 20,000 employees:
Now the 19,900 non-users, of whom a 98%-specific test still falsely accuses 2%:

About 20%. Of every 497 positive results, roughly 398 belong to people who never used anything. At a 0.5% base rate, even a test that sounds nearly perfect produces four false accusations for every true one.

This is why defensible testing programs never act on a single screening positive: the sample is split at collection, and a positive screen goes to a confirmatory method (like GC-MS) with a much higher specificity before any consequence. Firing on the screening result alone means accepting that most of the people you fire over a year will be innocent. Show HR the 99-versus-398 split — it tends to slow the meeting down.

Our fraud vendor says their model catches 95% of fraud and has only a 1% false-alarm rate, so '95% of the alerts it raises are real fraud'. Fraud is about 0.1% of our transactions. Our analysts say they are drowning in false alerts. Who is right?

Your analysts are right, and the vendor is committing the classic inversion: they are quoting P(alert | fraud) as if it were P(fraud | alert).

Run 100,000 transactions through their own numbers. About 100 are fraud, and the model catches 95 of them. The other 99,900 are legitimate, and a 1% false-alarm rate on that mountain is 999 false alerts. So the alert queue holds 95 real frauds buried in 999 false ones — precision of about 95 / 1,094, roughly 8.7%, not 95%.

Nothing here is contradictory: a model can be excellent by the vendor's two metrics and still produce a queue that is over 90% noise, purely because fraud is rare. When you evaluate alerting systems, the number your team lives with is precision at your base rate. Ask every vendor the same question: 'At our fraud rate, out of 100 alerts, how many are real?' Make them answer with counts, not percentages of percentages.

A well-known puzzle from medicine: a condition has prevalence 1%. A test detects 90% of cases, and 9% of healthy people also test positive. A woman tests positive. Most people (including many doctors, apparently) guess the chance she has the condition is around 90%. What is it really?
Per 10,000 women screened:
And the healthy majority contributes positives at 9%:

About 9.2% — not 90%. Of 981 positive results, only 90 are true cases; 891 are false alarms from the 9,900 healthy women.

You are remembering the research correctly: when this exact problem was put to physicians (in Gerd Gigerenzer's studies), the most common answer was around 90%, because the eye goes to the sensitivity and skips the base rate and the false positives entirely. The fix that reliably works — for doctors and everyone else — is translating percentages into natural frequencies: 'of every 1,000 women, 10 have it and 9 of them test positive; of the 990 without it, about 89 also test positive.' Counts make the right answer almost visible; percentages hide it.

Back to the 1%-prevalence screening test (99% sensitive, 95% specific). I tested positive, so we know the positive pool is 99 true cases and 495 false alarms per 10,000. Now a second, different confirmatory test — 99% sensitive and 99% specific — also comes back positive. What is my probability now?
The second test does not start from 1% — it starts from the pool the first test produced: 99 sick and 495 healthy per 594 positives. Run that pool through the confirmatory test:

About 95.2%. The first positive lifted your probability from 1% to 16.7%; the second, acting on that enriched pool, lifts it to roughly 95%.

This is the machinery behind 'screen, then confirm': sequential tests multiply evidence because each positive raises the base rate the next test works on. One honest caveat: the arithmetic assumes the two tests make independent errors. If both tests are fooled by the same biological quirk in the same patient, the real gain is smaller than 95% suggests — which is why good confirmatory tests are built on a different principle than the screen, not just a rerun of it.
Why does the exact same blood test result mean something completely different at a routine physical versus at a specialist's office? It feels like the test should just mean what it means.

Because a test result is a multiplier applied to a starting probability, and the two settings start from very different places.

Take a test that is 99% sensitive and 95% specific. At a routine physical, the people tested are mostly healthy walk-ins; suppose 0.2% actually have the condition. Per 10,000 tested: 20 cases, about 19.8 detected — against 499 false positives from the 9,980 healthy people (5% of them). A positive means roughly 19.8 / 518.8, about 3.8%.

At the specialist's office, patients arrive with symptoms and referrals; suppose 30% have the condition. Per 10,000: 3,000 cases producing 2,970 true positives, against 350 false positives from 7,000 healthy patients. A positive now means 2,970 / 3,320, about 89.5%.

Same test, same result, 3.8% versus 89.5%. The difference is that symptoms and referral patterns are themselves evidence — they quietly raised the pre-test probability before the lab did anything. When a clinician 'interprets the test in context', this arithmetic is the context.

A startup sells a home test advertised as '99% sensitive and 99% specific' for a condition that affects about 1 in 10,000 people. I bought one and tested positive. The box makes it sound nearly conclusive. What is the actual chance I have the condition?
Per 1,000,000 users — we need a big denominator because the condition is so rare:
Now the healthy 999,900, of whom a 99%-specific test still falsely flags 1%:

About 0.98% — roughly 1 in 100 positives is real, even with a genuinely excellent test. The false positives generated by the enormous healthy majority (9,999 of them) swamp the 99 true positives from the tiny affected minority.

This is not an argument that the test is bad; it is an argument about who should take it. Aimed at a high-risk group — people with symptoms or family history, where prevalence might be 1 in 50 — the same test is decisive. Sold to everyone, it mostly manufactures anxious false positives at scale, each of which then needs clinical follow-up to resolve. Whenever a test is marketed to the general public for something rare, do this division before you do anything else.

In a trial, the prosecutor says: 'The chance that an innocent person's DNA matches the crime-scene sample is 1 in a million. The defendant matches. So there is a 99.9999% chance he is guilty.' The city has about 5 million people. Take his argument apart with numbers.
The 1-in-a-million figure is P(match | innocent). The conclusion needs P(innocent | match) — a different quantity. Start with how many matches the city itself should contain:
About 5 other people in the city would also match, by the prosecutor's own figure. So the match evidence points at a pool of roughly 5 + 1 people:

Given nothing but the DNA match, the defendant is one of about 6 matching people — a probability of guilt around 1/6, or 17%, not 99.9999%.

This is the prosecutor's fallacy: swapping the direction of a conditional. P(match | innocent) being tiny does not make P(innocent | match) tiny when the population searched is huge, because rare events happen to someone in a big enough crowd. Of course, a real case never rests on the match alone — evidence placing the defendant near the scene, with motive and no alibi, legitimately shrinks that pool of 6 toward 1. But that shrinking must be done by the other evidence, argued explicitly. The match statistic by itself cannot carry the weight the prosecutor put on it.
A family has two children, and one of them is a boy. What is the probability both children are boys? I say 1/3, my friend says 1/2, and we have a small bet riding on who is right.

You may both owe each other a drink, because the honest answer is: it depends on how you came to know that one is a boy — and the bet turns on that detail, not on the arithmetic.

Version one: all you know is 'at least one of the two is a boy.' The equally likely families are BB, BG, GB, GG. The information rules out GG, leaving three families, one of which is BB — probability 1/3. Your answer.

Version two: you know something about a specific child — the older child is a boy, or you met one of them at the door and it was a boy. Now the other child is simply a fresh 50/50, and the probability both are boys is 1/2. Your friend's answer.

The lesson generalizes far beyond this puzzle: a conditional probability is only defined once you specify exactly what was conditioned on and how that information was selected. 'Given that one is a boy' sounds like one fact but is two different sampling procedures wearing the same sentence. When a conditional probability seems paradoxical, write down the procedure that produced the information before arguing about the fraction.

Harder version of the two-child puzzle: a family has two children, and at least one is a boy born on a Tuesday. What is the probability both are boys? I am told the answer is neither 1/3 nor 1/2, which sounds impossible — what does the day of the week have to do with anything?

It sounds absurd, but the specificity of the information genuinely matters. Give each child 14 equally likely descriptions: boy/girl crossed with 7 birth days. First, the probability that a two-child family has at least one Tuesday-born boy. For one child, the chance of NOT being a Tuesday boy is 13/14:

So about 13.8% of families (27/196) meet the condition. Now the numerator: both children are boys (probability 1/4), and at least one of them is Tuesday-born. For a boy, the chance of not being born on Tuesday is 6/7:
That is 13/196 of all families. Divide the favorable families by the conditioned families:

13/27, about 48.1% — much closer to 1/2 than to 1/3.

Why does an irrelevant detail move the answer? Because 'a boy born on Tuesday' nearly identifies which child you are talking about. In most families satisfying the condition, the Tuesday boy is a specific, singled-out child, and the other child is then a fresh coin flip — the situation from the 1/2 version of the puzzle. The plain 'at least one boy' version (1/3) gives you no handle on which child, so both-boy families are diluted by the boy-girl and girl-boy families. Conditioning is always relative to exactly what was specified: the more specific the stated fact, the more it behaves like pointing at one child. It is a strange result, but every step is forced.

We run two servers, each with about a 2% chance of failing on any given day. I calculated the chance both fail on the same day as 0.02 x 0.02 = 0.04% and called it negligible. My boss says the real figure is much higher. Who is right, and why?

Your multiplication is correct arithmetic applied to an assumption you have not checked: independence. Watch what the joint probability becomes if the two servers share something. Suppose both hang off the same power feed and network switch, and that shared infrastructure fails on about 1% of days, taking both down together:

Your boss is right. The independence answer is 0.04%. With a shared cause in the picture, the joint failure probability is P(shared failure) + P(no shared failure) x P(both fail independently) = 0.01 + 0.99 x 0.0004, about 1.04% — roughly 26 times your figure.

The multiplication rule P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B) is a theorem about independent events, not a law of nature about pairs of things. Real systems are dense with shared causes: same power, same rack, same deploy pipeline, same upstream provider, same on-call human. In reliability work, the independence assumption is the single most common source of wildly optimistic numbers. Before multiplying, ask what could take both down at once — that list, not the product of the marginals, sets your real risk.
Explain the Monty Hall problem so it actually convinces me. Three doors, I pick one, the host opens a different door showing a goat, and I am told switching wins 2/3 of the time. I do not feel it.

Forget formulas; just follow the car. You pick door 1. The car is equally likely to be behind door 1, 2, or 3, so consider the three cases, each with probability 1/3.

Car behind door 1: the host opens a goat door (say 2). If you switch to door 3, you lose. Car behind door 2: the host cannot open door 2 (car) or door 1 (your pick), so he must open door 3. Switching takes you to door 2 — you win. Car behind door 3: the host must open door 2, switching takes you to door 3 — you win.

Switching wins in two of the three equally likely cases: 2/3. The intuition to hold onto is that your first pick had a 1/3 chance, and that never changes — the host's performance cannot move probability onto or off of a door he never touches. The other 2/3 was spread over doors 2 and 3, and the host, who knows where the car is, concentrates all of it onto the one door he leaves closed. His choice is not random; it leaks information.

If the 3-door version still feels slippery, scale it: 100 doors, you pick one, the host opens 98 goat doors. Your door was a 1-in-100 shot. The survivor door carries the other 99/100. Almost everyone switches then — and it is the same problem.

Our churn analysis found that 80% of churned customers had opened a support ticket in the previous quarter. The product VP concludes tickets drive churn and wants to make support harder to reach so fewer tickets get filed. Our churn rate is 5%, and 30% of customers open a ticket in a quarter. Stress-test the VP's logic.
The VP is reading a conditional backwards. '80% of churners had tickets' is P(ticket | churn). The claim needs P(churn | ticket). Per 10,000 customers:

Customers who opened tickets churn at 13.3%; customers who did not churn at about 1.4%. Tickets are indeed associated with churn — but the direction of the story matters. The natural reading is that trouble causes both: a customer whose integration breaks or whose bill is wrong opens a ticket AND starts shopping for alternatives. The ticket is the smoke, not the fire.

Making support harder to reach would suppress the smoke signal while the fire burns on — and plausibly raises churn, since struggling customers now struggle alone. If the VP wants causality, the test is not fewer tickets; it is comparing churn between customers whose ticketed problems got resolved and customers whose did not. Association between a distress signal and a bad outcome is usually a reason to fund the signal's department, not to blind it.

A study of hospital patients found that among admitted patients, having condition A makes you LESS likely to have condition B. In the general population the two conditions are independent. Nobody faked the data. How can both be true?

This is Berkson's paradox, and the culprit is the doorway into the dataset: admission to hospital is caused by having A or by having B (or many other things). Conditioning on admission tangles the two conditions together.

Strip it to a toy. Population 10,000; A affects 10%, B affects 10%, independently — so 100 people have both, 900 have A only, 900 have B only, 8,100 have neither. Now impose the crudest admission rule: you are in the study if you have A or B (the hospital admits the sick). The study population is 1,900 people. Among admitted patients with A (1,000 of them), only 100 have B — 10%. Among admitted patients without A, all 900 have B — 100%, because B is the only way they got in. Inside the hospital, A and B look strongly negatively associated; outside, they are independent. Real admission rules are softer, so the real effect is weaker, but the direction survives.

The general shape: whenever your sample is selected on a common consequence of two variables (admission, hiring, being in the dataset at all), the variables will appear related inside the sample even if they are unrelated outside it. Before believing any association, ask: how did these rows get here, and what did entry require?

A vendor brochure says 'every component is 90% reliable'. Their system needs all three components working in series. A rival design runs three components in parallel so any one working is enough. What are the actual system reliabilities in each design?
Series first — the system works only if every component works, so the reliabilities multiply:
Parallel — the system fails only if all three fail together:

Series: 0.9 x 0.9 x 0.9 = 72.9%. The brochure's '90% reliable' quietly describes a component, while the customer experiences the system — three honest 90s compound into a mediocre 73%.

Parallel: 1 - 0.1^3 = 99.9%. The same mediocre components, arranged so their failures must coincide, produce an excellent system. Architecture dominates component quality: redundancy converts multiplication of success probabilities into multiplication of failure probabilities.

One caveat before you quote 99.9% to anyone: both calculations assume the components fail independently. Shared power, shared software, or a shared environment correlates the failures and eats the redundancy gain — the parallel figure is a ceiling, reached only when the failure modes are genuinely separate.
Our service has about a 1% chance of an outage on any given day. A teammate argues that means a 30% chance of at least one outage this month — 30 days times 1%. Is that right?
Close, but the addition double-counts. The clean way is through the complement: the chance of no outage on a given day is 0.99, so the chance of a clean month is:

About 26%, not 30%. The '30 x 1%' shortcut counts every outage day separately — including the worlds where two or three outages happen in the same month, which the phrase 'at least one' should only count once. The gap between the shortcut and the truth is exactly those overlapping worlds.

The reliable pattern is: P(at least one) = 1 - P(none). Reach for it whenever events can repeat — outages, defects, rainy weekends. The additive shortcut is only a decent approximation when the probability is tiny AND the window is short, and even then it always overstates.
An article profiles successful founders and notes that 90% of them wake up at 5 a.m. I have started setting my alarm. A statistician friend is unimpressed. Why?

Because the article measured P(5 a.m. | successful) and you are acting on P(successful | 5 a.m.), and those two numbers can be arbitrarily far apart.

To convert one into the other you would need two things the article does not have: the base rate of success among founders, and the share of ALL founders — including the failed and the never-profiled — who wake at 5 a.m. If 90% of all founders are early risers (plausible; running out of money concentrates the mind at dawn), then the successful group shows exactly the population rate and the fact carries zero information. If only 20% of all founders rise at 5, the same statistic would be real evidence. The article cannot distinguish those worlds, because it never looked at the failures.

That is survivorship in its most everyday costume: we interview the winners, catalogue their habits, and sell the catalogue as causes. The unsuccessful majority had alarm clocks too. Set your alarm if mornings suit you — but know the statistic you read is compatible with the habit being anything from decisive to irrelevant.

A carnival game costs $5 a roll. Roll a 6 and you win $12; roll a 5 and you win $6; anything else you win nothing. The operator says people win all the time. Is it worth playing if I care about the money?
'People win all the time' is true — a third of rolls pay something. The question is the average. Each face has probability 1/6, so the expected payout is:

Expected payout per roll is $2 + $1 = $3, against a $5 price — an expected loss of $2 every roll. The game is engineered so that winning feels frequent (two of six faces pay) while the amounts guarantee the operator's margin: frequency of winning and profitability of playing are completely separate things.

Expected value is the right lens for anything you will repeat: play this 100 times and you should expect to be down about $200, give or take the luck of the run. A single roll proves nothing either way — you might hit two sixes — but the average is a tide, and tides win over evenings.

A store offers a $129 protection plan on a $1,200 laptop. There is about an 8% chance of a failure in the next 3 years that would cost $450 to repair. Break down the expected value for me, and also explain why the store is so keen to sell these plans.
Your expected repair cost without the plan is the failure probability times the repair bill:
$36 of expected cost versus a $129 price. But the spread matters as much as the mean. The standard deviation of your single outcome (pay $450 with probability 0.08, else $0) is:
Now look at the store's side. Selling 10,000 plans, their average claim cost per plan has a standard deviation of that figure divided by the square root of 10,000 — that is, by 100:

For you: expected repair cost $36, plan price $129. As a pure investment the plan loses about $93 on average — but your outcome is a single draw with a standard deviation of about $122, meaning the real choice is between a certain $129 and a small chance of a $450 bill at an inconvenient moment. That insurance against timing is the only thing being sold, and whether it is worth it depends on whether $450 would hurt.

For the store it is a different universe: across 10,000 plans their average cost per plan is $36 give or take about $1.22, against $129 of revenue each — $1.29 million in, roughly $360,000 out in expected claims. Pooling converts your gamble into their near-certainty. Insurance is the business of buying variance cheaply from many people who each find it expensive to hold alone.
I found a bet that wins 55% of the time at even money — clearly positive expected value. My plan: bet my whole bankroll each time and let it ride. Guaranteed riches eventually, right?
The edge is real. Per $1 staked, your expected profit is:
But 'let it ride' has a hidden requirement: you must win every single bet, because one loss zeroes you. The probability of surviving 10 consecutive all-in bets is:
Compare a dull alternative: stake 10% of the current bankroll each time. Even five straight losses — a bad week — leaves you with:

Positive expected value, and a 99.75% chance of being broke within 10 bets. Both statements are true, and the second one is the one that will happen to you.

Expected value averages over parallel universes; ruin is absorbing — once you hit zero, the average of the other universes stops paying your rent. This is why stake sizing is a separate discipline from edge-finding (the Kelly criterion is its formal version): bet a fraction small enough that losing streaks are survivable, and the edge compounds; bet the roll, and the edge is a lottery ticket on never being unlucky. A 55% bettor staking 10% keeps about 59% of the bankroll even after five straight losses — battered, but still in the game where the 55% can work. The graveyard of betting is full of people who were right about the odds.
Is a $2 lottery ticket ever worth it mathematically? Say the jackpot is $5 million and the odds of winning it are 1 in 10 million.

As an investment, no, and it is not close. The jackpot's contribution to the ticket's expected value is $5,000,000 x 1/10,000,000 = $0.50. Add the small prizes — suppose 1 ticket in 100 wins $5 back, contributing another $0.05 — and the ticket's expected value is roughly $0.55 against its $2 price. You are paying about $1.45 per ticket for something other than money: a day of pleasant what-if. (And on the rare occasions the jackpot is won, it is often split, which lowers the true figure further.)

None of that makes buying one irrational — entertainment is a legitimate purchase, and $2 for a daydream is cheap compared to a movie. The error is only in the accounting: file it under entertainment, like the movie. The people lotteries actually harm are the ones filing it under 'retirement plan' and buying in bulk, because expected value scales linearly: a hundred tickets a week is just the same -72% return with a bigger budget.

Two health plans. Plan A: $900/year premium, no deductible. Plan B: $500/year premium, but I pay the first $1,000 of any incident myself. My chance of having an incident in a year is about 12%. Which is cheaper in expectation — and what is the catch?
Plan B's hidden premium is the expected deductible you will actually pay:
And the break-even incident probability — the point where the plans tie — is:

In expectation, Plan B costs $620 a year against Plan A's $900 — B wins by about $280 a year at your 12% incident rate. The plans would tie only if your yearly incident probability were 40%, far above your estimate.

Now the catch, and it is the standard one: expected value flattens the timing. Plan A's $900 leaves in calm monthly installments. Plan B's cost, when it comes, arrives as a $1,000 lump in the same month you are sick or injured. If that lump would go on a credit card at 25% interest, the real price of B rises; if you hold a decent emergency fund, B's $280 edge is real money. Expected value picks the winner on average — your balance sheet decides whether you can afford to play the average.

I can invest $50,000 in a project: 60% chance it returns $120,000, 40% chance it returns only $10,000. Or I can sell the idea today for a certain $65,000. Compare them properly, and tell me where the decision flips.
Expected value of the project first:
Now solve for the success probability at which the project merely ties the certain $65,000 — that is where (120,000 - 10,000) x p = 65,000 - 10,000:
And sanity-check just below the flip point, at 45%:

The project's expected value is $76,000 — an expected gain of $26,000 over your stake — against a certain $65,000. On expected value alone, investing wins by $11,000.

But the distribution deserves a sentence before you sign: there is a 40% chance you end with $10,000, i.e. $40,000 poorer than your stake and $55,000 poorer than the sure thing. The flip point is a 50% success probability: above it the project's EV beats the offer, below it the offer wins (at 45%, EV is $59,500 and selling is correct). So the real work is not this arithmetic — it is interrogating the 60%: where did it come from, and how much do you trust it? EV tells you how to decide once the probabilities are on the table; it cannot certify the probabilities. And if the $40,000 loss branch would genuinely damage you, taking the certain $65,000 is not a math error — it is buying your way out of a tail you cannot afford.
Settle an argument: my co-founder says if a bet has positive expected value, taking it is always the rational move, full stop. I say there are exceptions. Who is right?

You are. Expected value is the average over many repetitions, and it quietly assumes you get to keep playing. Three common situations break it.

First, ruin: a bet that pays +$50,000 with 99% probability and costs you your $300,000 house with 1% probability has EV = 0.99 x 50,000 - 0.01 x 300,000 = 49,500 - 3,000 = +$46,500. Positive — and a terrible bet for almost anyone, because the losing branch ends the game: you cannot average your way out of homelessness across parallel universes. Second, one-shot decisions: EV is a long-run average, and a single unrepeatable choice has no long run; the distribution, not the mean, is what you will actually live in. Third, diminishing utility: the thousandth dollar is worth less to you than the dollar that pays rent, so equal expected dollars are not equal expected wellbeing — this is the entire reason sane people buy insurance with negative EV.

The clean rule: expected value governs repeated, survivable, roughly independent bets. Outside that territory — ruin on the table, one throw only, stakes that are large relative to your wealth — maximize something closer to expected utility, or growth rate, and let EV be one input rather than the verdict.

Our A/B test showed conversion rising from 2.0% to 2.2%, with 50,000 visitors in the variant group. Average margin is $30 per order. What is the rollout worth per month at this level of traffic, roughly?

The arithmetic is quick. The lift is 0.2 percentage points, which is 0.002 as a fraction. On 50,000 visitors a month, that is 50,000 x 0.002 = 100 extra orders, and at $30 margin each, about $3,000 per month, or $36,000 a year if it holds.

Now the honesty clause, because the number deserves one: a 0.2-point difference measured on 50,000 visitors per group carries a standard error of roughly 0.09 points, so the observed lift is only about 2.2 standard errors from zero — suggestive, not iron-clad, and the true lift could plausibly be anywhere from nearly nothing to about twice the point estimate. Treat $3,000/month as the center of a range, not a promise: worth rolling out if the change is cheap and reversible, worth another week or two of data if the rollout is expensive. When someone asks 'what is it worth', the complete answer is always a number plus the width of the uncertainty around it.

A game costs $10 to play. Payouts: 50% chance of $8, 30% chance of $15, 20% chance of $40. Give me the expected value and some sense of the spread — I want to know what a single evening of playing looks like, not just the average.
Expected payout, term by term:
For the spread I need E[X^2] as well:

Expected payout is $16.50 against a $10 ticket — a genuinely favorable game, +$6.50 per play on average. But the standard deviation of a single play is about $12.13, nearly twice the edge. That is the answer to your real question: in one evening of, say, ten plays, the average will not have asserted itself yet — outcomes tens of dollars either side of the +$65 expectation are perfectly ordinary, because the per-play noise ($12) shrinks only with the square root of the number of plays.

This is the two-number discipline: never quote an expected value without its spread. EV tells you which side of the game to be on; the standard deviation tells you how long and how bumpy the ride to that average will be.
Explain the Kelly criterion idea to me without worshipping the formula. Concrete case: an even-money bet I win 60% of the time. Why not bet big?

Bet a fixed fraction f of your bankroll each time, and follow what a typical win-loss pair does to you. At f = 100%: one loss and you are at zero — done, edge or no edge. At f = 50%: a win then a loss multiplies you by 1.5 x 0.5 = 0.75 — you lost a quarter of your money on a sequence that contains exactly as many wins as losses. At f = 20%: 1.2 x 0.8 = 0.96. At f = 10%: 1.1 x 0.9 = 0.99.

Now run a realistic 10 bets at your true rate — 6 wins, 4 losses. At f = 50%: 1.5^6 x 0.5^4 = 11.39 x 0.0625 = 0.71 — you are down 29% while being right about the bet. At f = 20%: 1.2^6 x 0.8^4 = 2.99 x 0.41 = 1.22 — up 22%. At f = 10%: 1.1^6 x 0.9^4 = 1.77 x 0.66 = 1.16 — up 16%. The 20% bettor beats the 10% bettor beats the 50% bettor, and the 100% bettor is almost surely ruined. (For an even-money bet the growth-maximizing fraction works out to 2p - 1 = 20% here — but the shape of the lesson matters more than the formula: there is an interior optimum, and overbetting a genuine edge still loses.)

The deep point: losses and gains are asymmetric — a 50% loss needs a 100% gain to undo. Fractions near the optimum keep the drawdowns recoverable so the edge gets the thousands of repetitions it needs to express itself.
A poll of 1,000 voters puts support at 52%. The campaign is quoting a margin of error but nobody can tell me where it comes from. Also, what would a cheaper 400-person poll cost us in precision?
The margin of error for a proportion is 1.96 times the standard error, and the standard error is sqrt(p(1-p)/n). Worst case is p = 0.5, which is the convention for quoted margins:

At n = 1,000 the margin of error is about +/-3.1 percentage points: the honest statement is '52%, plausibly 49 to 55'. At n = 400 it widens to about +/-4.9 points.

Note the cruel geometry: precision improves with the square root of n, so halving the error bars costs four times the interviews. That is why professional polls cluster around n = 1,000 — it is the knee of the cost curve, buying +/-3 points before the price of precision turns savage. And remember what the margin does not cover: it assumes the sample was drawn randomly and that respondents resemble nonrespondents. It prices only the randomness of the draw, nothing else.

A gym chain surveyed 10,000 attendees of its 6 a.m. classes and found 92% approve of opening at 5 a.m. The margin of error is tiny, yet a membership-wide survey says approval is only 40%. How can a sample of 10,000 be that wrong with a straight face?
Let us first confirm the margin of error really is tiny:

The sampling noise is about +/-0.5 points, and the estimate is off by 52. Both facts coexist because the margin of error only measures one kind of error: the randomness of which population members happened to be sampled. It says nothing about whether the sampled frame matches the population you care about.

People at a gym at 6 a.m. are, by construction, the people who already come at 6 a.m. — the segment most likely to want an even earlier hour. The 40% figure comes from the whole membership, most of whom experience the gym at other times or barely at all. Total error = bias + noise. Noise shrinks with n; bias does not — surveying 10,000 of the wrong people, or 10 million, just estimates the wrong quantity with magnificent precision. A genuinely random sample of 400 members (+/-4.9 points, no bias) would have been worth far more than this census of the converted. Sample size is the least important property of a sample; who got in is the most important.

Our fund database reports that the average fund returned +10.3% a year over ten years. My analyst insists the true average investor experience was negative. The database only lists funds that still exist. Six surviving funds returned 12, 9, 15, 7, 11, and 8 percent. Four funds that were liquidated had returned -20, -35, -15, and -50 percent before they died. Settle it.
The database's number first — the survivors' average:
Now the funds the database quietly forgot:

Your analyst is right. The published average is +10.33%, but that is the average over the funds that survived to be counted. An investor choosing among all 10 funds ten years ago faced the full list, and its average is -5.8% a year. The database's editorial decision — list only the living — inflates the headline by about 16 points.

This is survivorship bias, and it infects far more than fund tables: business advice from companies that made it, 'what top performers do' studies, vintage strategy backtests. The failures are missing not at random but precisely because they failed, so the surviving average is a biased estimate of the prospects of the whole cohort. The first question to ask of any average is: who had to disappear for this number to look like this?
A survey firm mailed 50,000 questionnaires and got 2,000 back. They claim the margin of error is only +/-2.2% because n = 2,000. Something feels off. What is wrong with the claim?

The arithmetic is right and the claim is wrong, because the formula's fine print is doing all the work. The +/-2.2% figure assumes the 2,000 respondents are a random sample of the population. They are not: they are the 4% who chose to respond, and people who return questionnaires differ systematically from people who bin them — more free time, stronger opinions, more grievances, more enthusiasm. The 48,000 silent ones are not missing at random; their absence is data the formula ignores.

History's monument to this error is the Literary Digest poll of 1936: 2.4 million returned ballots predicted the wrong U.S. president, because the mailing lists (car and telephone owners during the Depression) skewed wealthy and the responders skewed further. A sample of 2.4 million lost to the truth; meanwhile modern polls with n = 1,000 random respondents routinely land within a few points.

The remedies are unglamorous: chase nonrespondents with follow-ups and compare them to respondents, weight the sample on known demographics, and treat a low response rate as a warning label, not a footnote. Precision is a property of the draw; accuracy is a property of the whole design. Vendors sell the first number and hope you never ask about the second.
How many people do we need to survey to pin support within +/-2 percentage points? And if the board demands +/-1 point, what does that cost?
Using the worst-case p = 0.5 and solving n = 1.96^2 x 0.25 / margin^2:

About 2,401 respondents for +/-2 points, and about 9,604 for +/-1 point. Halving the margin quadruples the sample — the square-root law again — which is why '+/-1%' polls are rare and expensive, and why most public polls settle for +/-3 at n near 1,000.

Two footnotes before you budget: these figures assume a true random sample with full response; real-world nonresponse means the fieldwork must start with a much larger contact list. And if the true proportion is far from 50% — say you are measuring something at 10% — the required n drops substantially, because p(1-p) shrinks. Design for the worst case when you do not know, but do not pay for the worst case when you do.

Our town is 70% urban and 30% rural. Support for the measure runs 50% among urban residents and 20% among rural ones. A convenience sample that ended up 95% urban reports 48.5% support and the campaign is celebrating. What is the true level of support, and can the same interviews be salvaged?
The true figure weights each group's support by its share of the town:
And the sample's mistake is visible by applying its own mix:

True support is 41%, not 48.5%. The convenience sample did not mishear anyone — urban and rural respondents answered as they answered. It simply interviewed the town in the wrong proportions: 95% urban in a town that is 70% urban, over-counting the supportive group by enough to manufacture a 7.5-point lead.

The salvage is post-stratification weighting: down-weight urban responses to their true 70% share and up-weight rural ones to 30%, and the same interviews reproduce the 41% — as just computed. Weighting is legitimate repair for skew you can measure (geography, age, sex — anything with known population shares). Its limit is equally important: it cannot fix skew on variables you did not record or do not know, and it cannot fix within-group bias — if the urbanites who answered differ from urbanites generally, no weights save you. Celebrate after the reweighting, not before.
Our app store page shows 4.8 stars across 30,000 reviews, and marketing wants to run 'Users rate us 4.8 out of 5' in an ad. As the resident skeptic, what do I say?

Say: 4.8 is the average of the reviews, not of the users, and those are different populations. Reviews are written by volunteers, and volunteering is not random: the delighted and the furious write; the vast, mildly satisfied middle — the typical user's actual experience — mostly does not. App ratings are famously J-shaped for this reason, a pile of 5s, a pile of 1s, and a valley where most users live.

Two more quiet distortions: the prompt matters ('Enjoying the app? Tap to rate' shown right after a success moment harvests a different sample than a prompt after a crash), and the pool drifts over time as unhappy users churn away and stop reviewing, so the average can rise while the product stands still. None of this means 4.8 is fabricated — it is a true fact about reviewers. If marketing wants a claim about users, the honest route is to sample users at random, including the silent ones, and ask them; the number will be lower and less shiny, and it will mean what the ad says. If they will not do that, the defensible wording is '4.8-star average from 30,000 app-store reviews' — precise about whose opinion it is.

Two polls, each with n = 1,000: candidate A at 46%, candidate B at 44%. The headline says 'A takes the lead'. Each poll's stated margin of error is +/-3.1 points. Is the lead statistically meaningful?
The subtlety: the margin of error on a single share is not the margin on the difference between two independent polls. The difference wobbles from both sides, so its standard error combines the two:

The margin of error on the gap is about +/-4.4 points — larger than each poll's own +/-3.1, because errors in the two estimates stack rather than cancel. The observed lead is 2 points, well inside +/-4.4. The headline should read 'statistical tie', and the race could equally be B ahead by a couple of points.

This trips up nearly all horse-race coverage: a 2-point shift between two polls is usually reported as movement when it is mostly weather. (One refinement: within a single poll, A and B's shares are linked — a voter for A is not for B — so a within-poll gap has a smaller error than this two-poll calculation. But the moment the comparison crosses polls, the independent-errors math above is the honest one.) If you need to detect a 2-point lead, you need far larger samples, not louder headlines.
A fund advertises '+180% over the period shown', and the chart starts in March 2020. I feel manipulated but cannot articulate why. Arm me.

Your instinct is correct, and the mechanism has a name: window selection. March 2020 was the bottom of a crash. Starting any return chart at a trough mechanically inflates everything after it — the same fund measured from January 2020, or from the 2019 peak, would tell a far duller story with identical management. The data is accurate; the sample of time was chosen.

It is the temporal twin of cherry-picking respondents: just as a survey can be rigged by choosing who gets asked, a track record can be rigged by choosing when the clock starts. The defenses are standardized windows and context. Ask for: returns over fixed calendar periods (trailing 1, 3, 5, 10 years, each ending today); the full history including the drawdown into March 2020, not just the climb out of it; the maximum peak-to-trough fall along the way; and a benchmark index over the identical window — beating a rising tide is a different claim from beating the market. A manager who will only show you the chart that starts at the bottom is telling you, in advance, how they will report the next bad year.

We emailed a survey to 1,000 customers. Only 200 responded, and 60% of them approve of the change. Before we report 60%, our researcher phoned a random sample of 80 nonrespondents and found 35% approval among them. What is our best estimate of approval across all 1,000 customers?
Build the estimate from the two groups, weighted by their sizes. Respondents approving:
Nonrespondents are 800 of the 1,000, and the phone sample estimates their approval rate at 35%:
One more check — how much uncertainty does the small phone sample inject? Its margin of error:

Best estimate: about 40% approval — not 60%. The respondents were the happy minority; assuming they spoke for the silent 800 would have overstated approval by 20 points. The nonrespondent follow-up is the professional move here: a small, expensive sample of the missing group beats any amount of additional responses from the willing group.

Carry the uncertainty honestly, though: the 35% figure itself has a margin of about +/-10.5 points (n = 80 is small), which moves the overall estimate by roughly +/-8 points. So the report should read 'approximately 40%, plausibly 32-48%' — a range that firmly excludes the naive 60% while admitting its own width. That is what a defensible number looks like: corrected for the bias you found, and labeled with the doubt that remains.

Our 12-person team's salaries (in $k) are in the salaries table. HR told a union rep that 'average pay here is $63k'. The rep says the typical employee earns far less. Pull the numbers and tell me who is describing the data honestly.
Let me look at the distribution, not just the headline average:

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, ROUND(AVG(salary_k), 2) AS mean_k, MIN(salary_k) AS min_k, MAX(salary_k) AS max_k FROM salaries

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
n | mean_k | min_k | max_k
12 | 63.42 | 38 | 240
The mean really is about $63.4k — but look at the max. One salary is $240k while the rest sit between $38k and $60k. The median is the middle pair of the ordered values:

arguments.sql: SELECT salary_k FROM salaries ORDER BY salary_k LIMIT 2 OFFSET 5

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
salary_k
47
48

Both sides are quoting real numbers; they are answering different questions. The mean is $63.42k — but it is dragged upward by a single $240k executive salary in a team of twelve. The median is $47.5k: half the team earns less than that, and eleven of the twelve earn $60k or less.

For 'what does the typical employee earn', the median is the honest statistic whenever a distribution is skewed — the mean silently lets one outlier speak for everyone. The mean is not useless: multiplied by headcount it gives the payroll total, which is what budgets need. The dispute dissolves once each side says which question its number answers. When someone quotes you an average, ask 'mean or median?' — under skew, the gap between them is itself information.

The deliveries table has the times (in minutes) for our last 20 orders. Marketing wants to promise '90% of orders within X minutes'. Find X from the data, and give me the mean and median while you are at it.
First the overall picture:

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, ROUND(AVG(minutes), 2) AS mean_min FROM deliveries

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
n | mean_min
20 | 27.65
For the 90th percentile by the nearest-rank method, I need the 18th value of 20 when ordered (0.9 x 20 = 18):

arguments.sql: SELECT minutes FROM deliveries ORDER BY minutes LIMIT 1 OFFSET 17

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
minutes
38
And the median is the average of the 10th and 11th ordered values:

arguments.sql: SELECT minutes FROM deliveries ORDER BY minutes LIMIT 2 OFFSET 9

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
minutes
26
27

The promise should be '90% within 38 minutes'. The mean delivery time is 27.65 minutes and the median is 26.5 — but a promise is a statement about the tail, not the center, so it must be set from a percentile. Advertising the mean would mean roughly half your customers' lived experience is worse than the number on the banner, and the angriest experiences live in the slowest 10% that the mean barely notices.

Two working rules: quote operational promises in percentiles (p90, p95) because those are the numbers customers can hold you to, and keep watching the gap between median and p90 — when it widens, your process is not slowing down uniformly, it is developing a failure mode at the edge.

HR computed the average employee commute from the commutes table as 35 minutes and drafted a remote-work policy around 'the typical 35-minute commute'. The table has a mode column nobody looked at. Check their work.
Their average first, then the split they skipped:

arguments.sql: SELECT ROUND(AVG(minutes), 1) AS overall_avg FROM commutes

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
overall_avg
35

arguments.sql: SELECT mode, COUNT(*) AS n, ROUND(AVG(minutes), 1) AS avg_min FROM commutes GROUP BY mode ORDER BY mode

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
mode | n | avg_min
bus | 5 | 48
car | 5 | 22

HR's arithmetic is impeccable and their conclusion is empty. The overall average really is 35.0 minutes — but there is no 35-minute commuter in the building. Drivers average 22 minutes; bus riders average 48. The distribution has two humps, and the mean sits in the valley between them, describing nobody.

A policy built on the blend misfires in both directions: it treats drivers as more burdened than they are and bus riders — the group with the least schedule control and the most to gain from remote days — as less burdened than they are. Whenever a summary statistic will drive a decision about people, check whether the population is actually one population. If a grouping column exists, the grouped means are the minimum due diligence; a single average over a bimodal distribution is a fact about your spreadsheet, not about your workforce.
A news article about my street says 'the average home sale price was $510k last year'. Nine homes sold for around $300k and one mansion sold for $2.4M. Is the article's number wrong?

Not wrong — worse than wrong, technically right. Check it: 9 x $300k = $2.7M, plus the mansion's $2.4M is $5.1M, divided by 10 sales is exactly $510k. The mean is honestly computed. It is also a terrible description of what a house on your street costs, since nine of the ten sales were near $300k and the median sale price is about $300k.

The mean and the median answer different questions. The mean (total value divided by count) is the right number for the tax assessor, who cares about the aggregate base. The median is the right number for 'what does a typical house here sell for' — the question a reader naturally thinks was answered. One $2.4M outlier among ten sales moved the mean by 70% while moving the median not at all.

Rule of thumb for reading any reported 'average': if the underlying thing can have extreme values (prices, incomes, wealth, wait times), assume the figure is a mean, ask for the median, and treat a big gap between the two as the real story.
Our status page says average API latency is 277.6 ms, from the latencies table. Users insist the app feels fast except when it occasionally hangs. Both cannot be true... can they?
Let me verify the claimed average and then look at the shape underneath it:

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, ROUND(AVG(ms), 1) AS mean_ms FROM latencies

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
n | mean_ms
15 | 277.6
The middle value of the 15 ordered measurements (the 8th) is the median:

arguments.sql: SELECT ms FROM latencies ORDER BY ms LIMIT 1 OFFSET 7

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
ms
130
And the 90th percentile — nearest-rank position 14 of 15 — is:

arguments.sql: SELECT ms FROM latencies ORDER BY ms LIMIT 1 OFFSET 13

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
ms
380

Both are true, and the users are describing the distribution more faithfully than the status page. The mean really is 277.6 ms — but the median request takes 130 ms. The typical experience is fast. The mean is inflated by the tail: a 380 ms response at p90 and one 1,980 ms monster that alone contributes more to the average than the eight fastest requests combined.

Latency is the classic skewed metric: bounded below by zero, unbounded above, so the mean always reports the tail's opinion. The honest status page shows the median for 'typical' and p90/p99 for 'bad' — 'median 130 ms, p90 380 ms' tells an engineer exactly where to work and tells users their experience is believed. An average that contradicts everyone's experience is not a lie, but it is a choice of statistic that hides the only interesting thing in the data.

Two classes took the same test. Class A has 30 students and averaged 80. Class B has 10 students and averaged 60. The school reported the combined average as 70 — the average of 80 and 60. Is that right?

No — that is the average-of-averages error, and it silently assumes the two classes are the same size. The combined average has to be computed from totals, not from the two means: class A produced 30 x 80 = 2,400 points, class B produced 10 x 60 = 600 points, so the school-wide average is (2,400 + 600) / 40 students = 75, not 70.

The intuition: class A's average represents three times as many students, so it should pull the combined figure three times as hard — 75 sits three-quarters of the way from 60 toward 80, exactly as the sizes dictate. Averaging averages is only harmless when every group is the same size, which is precisely when nobody is tempted to do it. Any time you combine rates, percentages, or means across groups — schools, stores, months with different numbers of days — rebuild them from the underlying counts. If the counts are not available, the combined figure cannot be computed, and saying so is better than averaging the averages.

Two machines on our line both average 10 parts per hour. Machine X's last three hourly counts were 8, 10, 12. Machine Y's were 0, 10, 20. My supervisor says they are equivalent since the averages match. Are they?

They have the same mean and almost nothing else in common. Compute the spread. Machine X's deviations from 10 are -2, 0, +2; squared, that is 4, 0, 4; the variance is 8/3, about 2.67, so the standard deviation is about 1.6 parts. Machine Y's deviations are -10, 0, +10; squared, 100, 0, 100; variance 200/3, about 66.7; standard deviation about 8.2 parts — five times X's.

Now translate that into operations. X never strays far from plan: you can staff, schedule, and promise around it. Y produced nothing at all in one hour and double in another; downstream stations alternately starve and flood, and any buffer sized to the average overflows or idles half the time. For planning purposes Y is not a 10-per-hour machine — it is a coin flip between 0 and 20 that happens to average 10.

This is why 'average' is never a complete summary: a mean compresses a distribution into one number and discards exactly the information — the spread — that operations, risk, and anyone downstream actually live with. Whenever two options tie on the mean, the tiebreaker is the variance, and it is rarely a small difference.

The readings table holds temperature sensor data for a server room that should sit around 21.5 C. The monitoring dashboard is alarming: it shows a mean of 91.99 C. Is the room on fire, or is something wrong with the data?
Checking the dashboard's figure against the table first:

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, ROUND(AVG(celsius), 2) AS mean_all FROM readings

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
n | mean_all
13 | 91.99
The mean is real arithmetic on bad data. Two readings are physically absurd for this room (a 999 and a -40 — classic sensor glitch values). Filtering to the plausible range:

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, ROUND(AVG(celsius), 2) AS mean_clean FROM readings WHERE celsius BETWEEN -10 AND 100

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
n | mean_clean
11 | 21.54

The room is fine; the pipeline is not. All 13 readings average to 91.99 C only because two glitch values — 999 and -40, the fingerprints of a sensor or transmission fault — are each hundreds of degrees from the truth, and the mean obediently splits the difference. The 11 plausible readings average 21.54 C, exactly the expected room temperature.

Three lessons travel well beyond thermometers. First, sanity-filter sensor data at ingestion and log how much you excluded — silent filtering hides failing hardware. Second, for glitch-prone feeds the median is the safer default summary, because a median would have reported about 21.5 C even with the glitches included. Third, when a dashboard shows something physically alarming, verify the raw rows before evacuating the building: a mean is only as sane as its dirtiest input.
My daughter scored 82 on an exam. In her class of 20 students, 13 scored below her. The school reports she is at the 65th percentile, but she insists 'I got 82%, not 65%'. Who is confused?

Nobody — two different numbers are both being called by similar names. The 82 is her score: the percentage of available points she earned, a comparison between her paper and the exam. The 65th percentile is a rank: the percentage of students who scored below her, 13 out of 20, a comparison between her paper and everyone else's.

The two can diverge wildly. On a brutal exam where the top score is 70, a student with 61% could sit at the 90th percentile. On an easy exam, 95% correct might be only the 60th percentile. Percent describes performance against the material; percentile describes performance against the cohort.

The practical upshot: percentile is the number that matters for anything competitive — admissions, honors cutoffs, norm-referenced scholarships — because those are rationed by rank. Percent is the number that matters for mastery: did she learn the material? A school reporting both is not contradicting itself; it is answering two different questions, and it should label them clearly enough that a smart kid does not think she is being short-changed.
When someone hands me a summary of a dataset and it just says 'the average is X', what should I demand before I trust it or act on it? Give me the checklist.

Five demands, in the order I would make them.

One: mean or median? Under skew they diverge, and the gap between them is diagnostic — a mean far above the median means a heavy right tail is doing the talking. Two: how many observations? An average of 6 and an average of 6,000 wear the same typography and deserve completely different confidence. Three: what is the spread — standard deviation, or better, the quartiles? The middle 50% tells you what 'typical' spans; two datasets with the same center and different spreads need different decisions. Four: what was excluded, and why? Outliers removed, nonrespondents dropped, dead funds delisted, glitch values filtered — every average is computed over a chosen subset, and the choice is where the bias lives. Five: what is the shape — one hump or two? A bimodal distribution's center describes nobody, and no single number will confess to it; ask for a histogram or at least the grouped means.

Underneath all five is one principle: a summary statistic is a compression, and compression is lossy by design. Your job is to find out what was thrown away and whether the decision you are about to make needed it.

Our top sales rep just posted a 140 quarter when the team mean is 100. Management is forecasting her at 140 again next quarter. Quarterly scores here have a test-retest reliability of about r = 0.5. What is the honest forecast, and why do 'star' quarters so rarely repeat?
The forecast is a regression calculation: expected next score = mean + r x (observed - mean). Her excess over the mean is 40, and only the reliable fraction of it is expected to persist:

Forecast about 120, not 140. An observed score is skill plus luck — territory, timing, a couple of big deals landing inside the quarter. Management selected the rep with the most luck stacked on top of skill, because that is what 'top of the table' means. The skill component (the part correlated across quarters, captured by r = 0.5) persists; the luck component re-rolls from zero.

So the expected repeat performance keeps only half the excess: 100 + 0.5 x 40 = 120. Note she is still forecast to be the team's best or near it — regression to the mean is not 'she was never good'. It is the arithmetic fact that extreme observations are extreme partly by accident, and accidents do not keep appointments. Budget, quotas, and bonuses set off the 140 will manufacture a 'slump' out of pure statistics.

A company piloted a safety program at the 5 sites whose incident rate had spiked to 9% last quarter. Those sites' long-run rate is 5%. This quarter the pilot sites are at 7%, though the program was barely implemented. The program manager claims a 2-point win. Evaluate.
Decompose the spike first. The sites were chosen because they hit 9% against a long-run 5% — so the spike contains about 4 points of 'bad quarter' on top of their true level:
If the quarter-to-quarter reliability of site rates is around r = 0.5, the expected rate next quarter with NO program at all is the long-run mean plus the reliable fraction of the spike:

The expected no-program outcome is 7% — exactly what was observed. The '2-point win' is indistinguishable from pure regression to the mean: sites were selected because of an extreme quarter, extreme quarters are partly noise, and noise does not repeat.

This is the single most common way improvement programs counterfeit their results — choose the worst performers, apply anything (or nothing), and harvest the statistical rebound. It does not prove the program is useless; it proves this evaluation cannot tell. The honest designs: pilot at randomly chosen sites, or compare against equally-spiked sites that did not get the program, or model each site's expected regression from its own history and credit the program only with improvement beyond it. Until one of those is done, the correct report is 'pilot sites at 7%, consistent with regression alone; effect unknown'.
Why does the Rookie of the Year in sports so often have a noticeably worse second season? Is it the pressure, the fame, the contract?

Mostly, it is arithmetic wearing a narrative costume. The award does not go to the most skilled rookie; it goes to the rookie with the best observed season, which is skill plus luck — good health, favorable matchups, balls bouncing the right way, a hot streak in the voting month. Selecting the maximum of a noisy measure selects for luck as much as for talent.

Next season the talent is still there (probably improved, in fact), but the luck re-rolls at its average value of zero. Expected performance = true skill, which is below the award season's observed performance even if the player got better in the off-season. Hence the 'sophomore slump', the 'Sports Illustrated cover jinx', and the 'Manager of the Year curse' — one phenomenon with many jerseys.

Pressure and fame may add real effects at the margins, but they are not needed to explain the pattern, and they make a testable prediction the data usually rejects: if pressure were the cause, the decline should hit players who were merely famous, not precisely those whose rookie numbers most exceeded their underlying rates. Before reaching for psychology, subtract the regression. What is left is the part that needs explaining.

A tutoring company advertises: 'We select the weakest students — those scoring under 40, group mean 32 — and after our program they average 41. A 9-point gain!' The population mean on this test is 55, and the test's test-retest reliability is 0.6. Grade their evidence.
Apply the regression formula to their selected group. Expected retest score with no intervention at all is the population mean plus r times the group's deviation from it:

Pure regression to the mean predicts a retest average of 41.2 for this group with no tutoring whatsoever. The company is advertising 41 — a hair below the do-nothing forecast.

The mechanism is selection: a score under 40 means a weak student OR a decent student having a bad day — illness, guessing badly, a mis-bubbled section. On retest, the bad days do not repeat on schedule, so the group's average rises mechanically. Any program that recruits at the bottom of a noisy measure will 'work' by this arithmetic, which is why remedial-program marketing loves pre/post designs with no control group.

The verdict on the evidence: worthless as presented, in a precise sense — the observed gain is fully explained by the null hypothesis of no effect. The fix is equally precise: a control group of equally low scorers, randomly assigned to wait a term. If the tutored group beats 41.2 by a real margin, there is something to sell. Until then, the 9 points belong to statistics, not to the tutors.

The city installed cameras at the 10 intersections with the most crashes last year. Crashes at those intersections fell 30% this year, and the mayor is claiming the cameras work. Should I believe her?

Believe that crashes fell; reserve judgment on why. Those 10 intersections were selected because they topped last year's table — and a table-topping year is a mixture of a genuinely dangerous junction and a bad-luck year: an unusual cluster of accidents that randomness dealt to that corner. The dangerous part persists; the luck part does not. So a substantial fall was expected even if the cameras were decorative — regression to the mean, arriving right on schedule to be photographed with the mayor.

This exact trap has a name in road-safety research, because naive before/after studies at selected blackspots systematically overstate interventions. The credible evaluations do one of three things: compare against similar high-crash intersections that got no cameras; use several years of pre-data and shrink each site's 'true' rate toward the average (empirical Bayes) before computing the expected fall; or randomize the rollout order and compare early versus late sites.

None of this says cameras do not work — there are good controlled studies suggesting red-light cameras reduce certain crash types. It says this mayor's number, from this design, cannot distinguish camera effects from arithmetic. When an intervention is always applied at the worst point of a noisy series, improvement is the null hypothesis, not the finding.

Last year's top-performing fund manager beat the market by 8 percentage points. A newsletter forecasts her fund to beat the market by about 8 points again this year. I have read that year-to-year persistence of manager performance is weak — a reliability of maybe r = 0.2. What is the better forecast?

Apply the same regression logic you would apply to any noisy measurement: expected repeat = market + r x (observed excess) = 0 + 0.2 x 8 = about 1.6 points of expected outperformance — not 8. Roughly 80% of last year's margin is best explained as the year's luck: the sectors she happened to hold, the quarter her style was in fashion. Only the reliable sliver, the part that correlates with next year's result, should be carried into the forecast.

Notice this does not say she is unskilled — an expected +1.6 points a year, if real, is a fine manager. It says the newsletter's method (last year's number, repeated) is the forecast that maximizes disappointment. It is also why 'past performance is not indicative of future results' is printed on everything: it is not legal boilerplate, it is the regression formula in a trench coat. When you must forecast from a single extreme observation, shrink it toward the base rate by the reliability — and the weaker the persistence, the harder you shrink.

Suspicious pattern at my company: every process change 'works'. Leadership intervenes whenever a metric hits its worst point, the metric improves afterward, and the VP of Ops gets the credit. Is he a genius, or is something else going on?

Something else, most likely — he has built a machine for harvesting regression to the mean. If you always intervene at the extreme of a noisy metric, the next measurement improves with high probability no matter what the intervention was, because the extreme was partly a fluctuation and fluctuations pass. The VP does not need to be competent; the calendar does the work.

There are fingerprints. The interventions 'work' nearly 100% of the time, which real interventions in a complex business never do. The size of the 'win' correlates with how extreme the trigger was — the worse the dip, the bigger the recovery — which is the signature of noise mean-reverting, not of a fixed treatment effect. And nobody keeps the counterfactual log: the times a metric cratered, nobody intervened, and it recovered anyway. Those cases exist in every company's history and are never in the VP's deck.

The fair test is not to stop intervening — sometimes the dip is a real fire. It is to grade interventions properly: pre-commit the metric and the horizon before acting, compare against similar units left alone, and shrink the expected recovery by the metric's reliability before crediting anyone. A genuinely good operator will still show wins after that accounting. A regression farmer will show exactly zero — which is itself valuable information.

Eight students took a test twice; the scores are in the retest table (t1, t2). The top scorer dropped from 90 to 79 and the teacher is blaming complacency. Compute the test-retest correlation, and work out what retest score the 90 scorer was actually expected to get.
The correlation between the two sittings, computed from the table's aggregates:

arguments.sql: SELECT ROUND((AVG(t1 * t2) - AVG(t1) * AVG(t2)) / (SQRT(AVG(t1 * t1) - AVG(t1) * AVG(t1)) * SQRT(AVG(t2 * t2) - AVG(t2) * AVG(t2))), 3) AS r FROM retest

messages.content: And the means and standard deviations I need for the prediction:

arguments.sql: SELECT ROUND(AVG(t1), 2) AS mean_t1, ROUND(AVG(t2), 2) AS mean_t2, ROUND(SQRT(AVG(t1 * t1) - AVG(t1) * AVG(t1)), 2) AS sd_t1, ROUND(SQRT(AVG(t2 * t2) - AVG(t2) * AVG(t2)), 2) AS sd_t2 FROM retest

messages.content: The top scorer's first result in z-score units:
Regression says the expected second z-score is r times the first:
For symmetry, the weakest first score (52) and its expected retest:

The test-retest correlation is 0.686 — decent but far from perfect, so every extreme first score carries a large dose of day-specific luck. The 90 scorer's expected retest score was about 81, and she scored 79: entirely ordinary regression, no complacency required. Symmetrically, the weakest student (52) was expected to rise to about 63 with no intervention at all.

This is the pattern teachers, coaches, and managers misread daily: punish the 'slacker' whose peak reverts, praise the 'responder' whose trough rebounds, and build theories of motivation on top of a correlation coefficient. The correct reading of a two-score table starts with r. Whatever movement r predicts is weather; only movement beyond it is signal about the student.
A star performer's numbers have dropped from their peak. How do I tell a genuine decline from mere regression to the mean? I do not want to excuse a real problem, or chase a phantom one.

Four checks, in order. First, reconstruct the base: gather many periods before the peak. If the 'peak' was one quarter sitting on years of lower results, you selected an extreme and regression is the default explanation. If the high level was sustained for years, the peak is their level, and a drop is news.

Second, ask whether you are looking at them because of the peak. Selection is the engine of regression: the performer who comes to your attention via a record quarter is expected to fall back; one who comes via a routine review is not carrying the same statistical debt.

Third, quantify the expected fall and compare. With a reliability r, regression predicts a settle at mean + r x (peak - mean) relative to their own long-run average. Movement down to that level is weather. Movement through it — settling below their historical norm, or a level shift visible across many post-peak periods — is a genuine decline, and it deserves a real investigation.

Fourth, look for a mechanism with timing: a territory change, a lost client, a health issue, a competitor's launch — something that changed when the numbers changed. Regression needs no story; real declines usually have one, and the story should precede or coincide with the drop, not be invented after it. The discipline is symmetric: do not credit interventions for rebounds that regression predicts, and do not blame performers for falls it predicts either. Save your attention for the residual.

I read about a famous psychology finding: flight instructors noticed that after they praised a pilot for an exceptionally good landing, the next landing was usually worse — and after they screamed at a pilot for a bad landing, the next was usually better. They concluded punishment works and praise backfires. What is actually going on?

What is going on is regression to the mean, and the instructors had unknowingly run a perfect demonstration of it. A landing's quality is pilot skill plus that day's noise — wind, fatigue, distraction. An exceptionally good landing is one where the noise was favorable; it is praised. The next landing draws fresh noise, which is average on average, so it is worse — not because of the praise, but because the exceptional noise did not repeat. An exceptionally bad landing is one where the noise was terrible; it is screamed at; the next draws average noise and improves.

Put a number on it: if the correlation between consecutive landings is modest, say r = 0.3, then a landing 2 standard deviations above the pilot's norm predicts a next landing of only about 0.3 x 2 = 0.6 standard deviations above it. The fall from +2 to +0.6 feels like the praise ruined him. The rise from -2 to -0.6 feels like the screaming fixed him. Both are arithmetic.

Daniel Kahneman, who told this story about the Israeli Air Force, called it one of the most instructive moments of his career, because the instructors' theory was built entirely from real observations — every fact they cited was true. The error was causal, not empirical. Any feedback system that responds to extremes — and most management does — will 'discover' that punishment works and praise harms, forever, in every organization, until someone plots the correlation and does this subtraction.

My nephew analyzed six months of data in the monthly table and found ice-cream sales correlate with drowning deaths at r = 0.997. He wants to ban ice cream at the lake. Check his arithmetic, then check his reasoning.
His arithmetic first — the correlation between ice-cream sales and drownings:

arguments.sql: SELECT ROUND((AVG(ice_cream_k * drownings) - AVG(ice_cream_k) * AVG(drownings)) / (SQRT(AVG(ice_cream_k * ice_cream_k) - AVG(ice_cream_k) * AVG(ice_cream_k)) * SQRT(AVG(drownings * drownings) - AVG(drownings) * AVG(drownings))), 3) AS r_ice_drown FROM monthly

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
r_ice_drown
0.997
0.997 — he computed it correctly. Now the variable he did not look at: temperature against drownings:

arguments.sql: SELECT ROUND((AVG(temp_c * drownings) - AVG(temp_c) * AVG(drownings)) / (SQRT(AVG(temp_c * temp_c) - AVG(temp_c) * AVG(temp_c)) * SQRT(AVG(drownings * drownings) - AVG(drownings) * AVG(drownings))), 3) AS r_temp_drown FROM monthly

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
r_temp_drown
0.996

The arithmetic is flawless and the conclusion is unfounded. Temperature correlates with drownings at 0.996 — because hot months put more swimmers in the water for longer. Heat is the common cause: it drives ice-cream sales up and drowning exposure up, so the two effects march together without either causing the other. Banning ice cream would leave every swimmer exactly as wet, and the correlation would collapse next summer while the drownings continued.

This is the confounder pattern, and a near-perfect correlation provides zero protection against it — r measures how tightly two series move together, and says nothing whatsoever about what moves them.
